title: The Satan, the Serpent and the Devil
bigQuestion: How did a Hebrew word for "adversary" become the name of the Bible's great enemy of God?

story.title: Who Let Him In?
story.kicker: A student reading Job notices something odd: the satan walks into God's court as if he belongs there.
paragraphs: Maya had a reading assignment for her literature class: the first two chapters of the book of Job. She expected a simple story about a good man who suffers. She opened a Bible at her kitchen table in Joliet and started to read. By the sixth verse she had stopped and read the line again.

The story says the sons of God came to stand before the LORD. It sounds like a royal court, with officials reporting to their king. Then the text says the satan came along with them. Nobody throws him out. Nobody seems surprised. God even speaks to him first and asks where he has been.

Maya had always pictured Satan as a monster with horns, far from God. This figure seemed different. He talked like an official doing a job. He questioned whether Job was good only because life had been easy for him. God set limits on what he could do, and he obeyed them.

She showed her older brother, who was taking a course on the Hebrew Bible. He pointed to a small note at the bottom of the page. It said the Hebrew has "the satan", with the word "the", and that the word means adversary. "So is it a name or a job title?" Maya asked. Her brother smiled. "Scholars have written whole books on that question."

One of those scholars was Michael Heiser, who read the Bible in its ancient languages. In his book Demons (2020) he traced how this Hebrew word changed over time. This chapter follows that path. It starts with a word for an opponent. It ends with the names Satan and the devil in the New Testament.
story.think: Why might a small word like "the" change how a reader understands who a character is?

lessons.title: What Satan Means
lessons.mainIdea: In Hebrew, satan is an ordinary word that means adversary, someone who opposes or blocks another.
reading: Start with Numbers 22. A foreign prophet named Balaam rides his donkey toward Moab. The text says the angel of the LORD stood in the road "as an adversary" against him. The Hebrew word there is *satan*. Here the adversary is God's own messenger. He blocks the road to stop Balaam from doing wrong.

The same word is used for people. In 1 Samuel 29:4, Philistine commanders worry that David might become a satan against them in battle. In 1 Kings 11:14, God raises up Hadad the Edomite as a satan against King Solomon. In these verses the word just means an enemy or opponent. Nobody in them is a spirit being.

So satan in the Hebrew Bible is first a common noun, like the English word "opponent". It describes a role, not one fixed person. Anyone can be a satan to someone else: a soldier, a king or an angel. Scholars call this the word's plain *meaning*, and it is the starting point for everything else in this chapter.

Michael Heiser made this point in Demons (2020). He argued that readers should not bring the later picture of Satan back into every verse with this word. First, he said, ask who is opposing whom in that passage.

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning adversary or opponent; someone who stands against another
what a word says in its own language and setting, before later ideas are added

look.title: Four Adversaries
look.text: Numbers 22:22 — the angel of the LORD stands in the road as a satan against Balaam. 1 Samuel 29:4 — the Philistines fear David may be a satan against them. 1 Kings 11:14 — Hadad the Edomite is a satan against Solomon. Job 1:6 — the satan comes before the LORD with the sons of God.
look.prompt: In the first three verses, who is the adversary and who is being opposed? Which of the four seems different, and why?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean?
check.why: Satan is a Hebrew word for an adversary, someone who opposes another. Serpent is nachash and messenger is mal'ak.

check.q: In Numbers 22:22, who stands in the road as a satan against Balaam?
check.why: Numbers 22:22 says the angel of the LORD stood in the road as an adversary to block Balaam.

check.q: What did Heiser say readers should ask first when they meet this word?
choices: Who is opposing whom in that passage
How many horns the figure has
Whether the verse rhymes in Hebrew
check.why: In Demons (2020) Heiser urged readers to read the word in its own setting and ask who opposes whom, not to read the later picture back into it.

lessons.title: The Satan in God's Court
lessons.mainIdea: In Job 1–2 the satan is a member of God's heavenly court who questions whether Job serves God for nothing.
reading: Job 1:6 opens a heavenly scene. The sons of God come to present themselves before the LORD, and the satan comes among them. In Hebrew the word has the article: ha-satan, "the satan". Heiser and many other scholars read this as a title, like "the prosecutor" or "the challenger".

The setting is what Heiser called the *divine council*: God's heavenly court, where spirit beings stand before him. In Job, the satan reports that he has been roaming the earth. God points to Job as a man without equal. The satan answers that Job is good only because God protects him and his family.

God allows a test, but sets clear limits. In chapter 1 the satan may not touch Job himself. In chapter 2 he may not take Job's life. The satan can only act inside the bounds God gives. After chapter 2 he never appears in the book again.

Heiser argued in The Unseen Realm (2015) and Demons (2020) that this satan is not the devil of later writings. He saw an officer of the court doing a hard job, perhaps with a bad attitude. Many Christian readers have long read Job's satan as the devil himself. Both readings look closely at the same two chapters.

words.d: Heiser's term for God's heavenly court, the spirit beings who stand before God in texts like Job 1 and Psalm 82
a small word like "the"; in Hebrew it is attached to the front of a noun (ha-)
a Hebrew phrase for heavenly beings who serve in God's court

look.title: The Court Scene
look.text: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them.
look.prompt: The King James Version prints "Satan" as a name, while the Hebrew says "the satan". How might each choice shape what a reader pictures?

check.q: In Job 1:6, who comes before the LORD along with the satan?
check.why: Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the satan came among them.

check.q: What limit does God set on the satan in Job 2?
choices: He may not take Job's life
He may not speak to God again
He may not visit Job's friends
check.why: In Job 2 God allows the satan to touch Job's body but not to take his life.

check.q: How did Heiser read the satan in Job?
choices: As an officer in God's court, not the later devil
As the king of Tyre in disguise
As one of Job's three friends
As a human judge in Job's town
check.why: Heiser read ha-satan in Job as a council member acting as a challenger. Many Christian readers see the devil there instead.

lessons.title: An Accuser in Zechariah
lessons.mainIdea: In Zechariah 3 the satan accuses the high priest Joshua, and the LORD rebukes the accuser.
reading: Zechariah was a prophet in Jerusalem around 520 BCE. His people had come back from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding the temple. In Zechariah 3 he sees a vision set in a heavenly court. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD. The satan stands at his right hand to *accuse* him.

Joshua is wearing filthy clothes. In the vision, that dirt pictures the people's guilt. The satan's job seems to be to point it out. But the accuser does not get the last word. The LORD says, in the prophet's words, "The LORD rebuke you, O satan!" and calls Joshua a burning stick snatched from the fire.
Then the dirty clothes are taken off. Joshua is given clean robes and a clean turban. The vision says his guilt has been taken away. The scene moves from accusation to cleansing and a fresh start.

Like Job, this text uses the article: ha-satan. Heiser pointed out that in both books the satan acts inside God's court, as an accuser. In both, God has the final say. Readers have noticed that the accuser in Zechariah ends up rebuked, a step toward the enemy of God pictured in later writings.

words.d: to charge someone with doing wrong, as a prosecutor does in court
the chief priest of Israel's temple, who led its worship

look.title: Dirty Clothes, Clean Robes
look.text: Paraphrase of Zechariah 3:1–5: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD in dirty clothes. The satan stands at his side to accuse him. The LORD rebukes the satan. The dirty clothes are removed, and Joshua is dressed in clean robes and a clean turban.
look.prompt: What do the clothes stand for in this vision? What happens to the accuser's case by the end?

check.q: What is the satan doing in Zechariah 3?
choices: Standing at Joshua's side to accuse him
Guarding the gate of the temple
Leading the people back from Babylon
check.why: Zechariah 3:1 shows the satan standing at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him.

check.q: What happens to Joshua's dirty clothes in the vision?
choices: They are replaced with clean robes
They are burned on the altar
They are given to the satan
They are buried in the ground
check.why: In Zechariah 3:4–5 the dirty clothes are taken away and Joshua is dressed in clean robes, a sign his guilt is removed.

check.q: What do Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 have in common?
choices: Both say "the satan", an accuser in God's court
Both are set in the garden of Eden
Both describe the king of Tyre
check.why: Both texts use ha-satan, with the article, for an accuser who acts inside God's heavenly court.

lessons.title: Why "The" Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the Old Testament uses satan as a role or title, not as the personal name it becomes in the New Testament.
reading: In Hebrew, as in English, people's names usually do not take "the". Nobody says "the Moses" or "the Sarah". But Job and Zechariah say "the satan". Heiser argued in Demons (2020) that this small word is a clue. It shows the word is working as a *title*, a description of a role, not a *proper name*.

Think of "the judge" or "the coach". Those words tell you what a person does, not who the person is. Heiser read ha-satan the same way: the one whose job was to challenge. This is why he said the Old Testament does not use satan as a name the way the New Testament uses Satan.

One verse is harder. In 1 Chronicles 21:1 the word appears without "the": satan stood up against Israel and moved David to count the people. Many translations print it as the name Satan. Other scholars translate "an adversary", which could mean a human enemy or an unnamed spirit. The retelling of the same story in 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger moved David.

Readers handle this in different ways. Some see the Chronicler naming the devil for the first time. Others, Heiser among them, doubted the verse gives a personal name. The debate shows how much one small word can matter when reading ancient texts.

words.d: a word that names a role or job, such as "the judge"
a word that names one particular person or place, such as Moses or Jerusalem

look.title: Same Story, Two Tellings
look.text: Paraphrase of 2 Samuel 24:1: The LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he moved David to count the people. Paraphrase of 1 Chronicles 21:1: Satan (or "an adversary") stood up against Israel and moved David to count the people.
look.prompt: The two books tell the same event. What changes between them? Why might translators disagree about whether to write "Satan" or "an adversary"?

check.q: Why did Heiser think "the satan" in Job is a title?
choices: Hebrew names usually do not take "the"
The word is written in red ink
Job calls him by his first name
The word only appears in Greek
check.why: Heiser argued that the article "the" shows a role being described, since personal names normally do not take it.

check.q: Which verse uses the word without "the" and is debated?
check.why: 1 Chronicles 21:1 has satan without the article, so scholars debate whether it is the name Satan or "an adversary".

check.q: According to 2 Samuel 24:1, what moved David to count the people?
check.why: 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger burned against Israel and moved David. 1 Chronicles 21:1 tells the same event with satan.

lessons.title: From Satan to Devil
lessons.mainIdea: Greek translators turned satan into diabolos, "slanderer", which gave English the word devil.
reading: Around the 200s BCE, Jewish scholars began to translate the Hebrew Bible into Greek. That translation is called the *Septuagint*. In Job, the translators wrote ho diabolos for ha-satan. Diabolos means slanderer, someone who speaks lies or accusations against another.

The English word *devil* comes from diabolos. So does the Spanish diablo. When the New Testament was written in Greek, its writers used both words. Sometimes they wrote Satanas, the Hebrew word in Greek letters. Sometimes they wrote diabolos. By then both had become names for one enemy of God.

Revelation 12:9 pulls the names together in one line. It calls one figure the great dragon, the old serpent, the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. Heiser pointed to this verse in Demons (2020). He noted that the New Testament links the serpent of Eden with Satan and the devil, something the Old Testament never spells out.

So the path runs like this. A Hebrew word for adversary became a title in God's court. Greek translators rendered it slanderer. By the time of the New Testament, Satan and the devil were names for one leader of evil.

words.d: the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 200s BCE
from the Greek diabolos, slanderer; in the New Testament a name for Satan

look.title: All the Names at Once
look.text: And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.
look.prompt: List every name this verse gives the figure. Which one points back to Genesis 3?

check.q: What does the Greek word diabolos mean?
check.why: Diabolos means slanderer. The Septuagint used it for ha-satan in Job, and it gave English the word devil.

check.q: Which verse calls one figure the dragon, the old serpent, the devil and Satan?
check.why: Revelation 12:9 gathers all these names for one figure who deceives the whole world.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
A scroll of Enoch found near the Dead Sea
check.why: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 200s BCE.

lessons.title: The Serpent in Eden
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the serpent of Genesis 3 as a divine being in God's garden, whom the New Testament later calls Satan.
reading: Genesis 3 tells of a serpent in the garden of Eden. It speaks to the woman and questions God's command. The Hebrew word for serpent is *nachash*. Genesis 3 never calls it Satan. It is simply the serpent, more crafty than any creature God had made.

Heiser argued in The Unseen Realm (2015) that Eden was more than a garden. He read it as God's home on earth, where God met with his council. So he saw the serpent as a divine being, not just an animal. He noted that nachash is related to Hebrew words for shining and for divination. To him this hinted at a bright, heavenly figure.

In Heiser's reading, this being rebelled against God's plan for humans. His punishment was to be cast down to the ground, below the heavenly realm. Heiser called him the Eden *rebel*, and he saw him as the one the New Testament names Satan and the devil.

Other readers differ. Many Jewish readers treat the serpent as a clever animal in a story about human choices. Some scholars see it as a symbol of temptation. Many Christians, following Revelation 12:9 and Romans 16:20, identify it with Satan, as Heiser did, though not always for his reasons.

words.d: the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3
one who rises up against a rightful ruler; Heiser's term for the serpent who turned against God in Eden

look.title: Three Ways to Read the Serpent
look.text: Reading 1: The serpent is a clever animal in a story about human choice. Reading 2: The serpent is a symbol of temptation. Reading 3 (Heiser): The serpent is a divine being in God's garden who rebels and is cast down, later called Satan in the New Testament.
look.prompt: Which details in Genesis 3 might each reader point to? What would you want to check in the text?

check.q: What Hebrew word does Genesis 3 use for the serpent?
check.why: Nachash is the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3. Satan means adversary and diabolos is Greek for slanderer.

check.q: How did Heiser picture Eden?
choices: As God's home on earth where he met his council
As a city built by the king of Tyre
As a desert where Azazel lived
As a garden with no spirit beings in it
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015) Heiser read Eden as God's dwelling where his council met, so the serpent was a divine being.

check.q: How do many Jewish readers treat the serpent in Genesis 3?
choices: As a clever animal in a story about human choices
As the angel who blocked Balaam
check.why: Many Jewish readers see the serpent as a crafty creature in a story about human choice, while many Christians identify it with Satan.

lessons.title: The King of Babylon
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 14 is a taunt song against the king of Babylon, who is pictured as a shining star thrown down from heaven.
reading: Isaiah 14:4 tells Israel to take up a taunt song against the king of Babylon. A *taunt song* mocks a proud enemy who has fallen. The poem imagines the dead in the underworld stirring to greet this king. They say he has become as weak as they are.

Isaiah 14:12 calls the king helel ben shachar in Hebrew. That means "shining one, son of the dawn", likely the morning star we now know as the planet Venus. Modern translations often say Day Star or morning star. The King James Version used *Lucifer*, a Latin word for the morning star meaning light-bringer.

In the poem, the king says in his heart that he will climb to heaven. He will set his throne above the stars of God and sit on the mount of assembly in the far north. He wants to be like the Most High. Instead, he is brought down to the pit.

Scholars have noticed that this language fits old stories from Canaan and Ugarit. Those stories told of gods meeting on a mountain in the north. The poem borrows that picture of a heavenly council to show how far the proud king falls.

words.d: a poem that mocks a proud enemy who has been brought low
a Latin word for the morning star, meaning light-bringer; used in the KJV at Isaiah 14:12

look.title: The Fallen Star
look.text: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
look.prompt: Isaiah 14:4 says this poem is about the king of Babylon. What words in this verse picture him as a star?

check.q: According to Isaiah 14:4, who is the taunt song about?
check.why: Isaiah 14:4 says to take up this taunt song against the king of Babylon.

check.q: What does the Hebrew helel ben shachar mean?
choices: Shining one, son of the dawn
check.why: Helel ben shachar means shining one, son of the dawn, likely the morning star. The KJV used the Latin Lucifer.

check.q: Where does the king in the poem want to sit?
choices: On the mount of assembly in the far north
In the garden of Eden by the river
In the wilderness with a goat
At the gate of Tyre by the sea
check.why: Isaiah 14:13 has the king boast that he will sit on the mount of assembly in the far north, above the stars of God.

lessons.title: The King of Tyre
lessons.mainIdea: Ezekiel 28 speaks to the king of Tyre as if he had been a glorious being in Eden who fell through pride.
reading: Tyre was a rich port city on the coast of what is now Lebanon. Its merchants traded across the Mediterranean Sea. Around the 580s BCE, the prophet Ezekiel spoke against its king. In Ezekiel 28:2 the king claims, "I am a god; I sit in the seat of the gods." Ezekiel answers that he is only a man.

Then, in 28:12–19, Ezekiel sings a *lament*, a sad poem for the dead or the fallen. He says the king was in Eden, the garden of God. He was covered with precious stones. He is called an anointed *cherub* on the holy mountain of God. He was blameless until wrong was found in him.
His heart grew proud because of his beauty. His trade filled him with violence. So God cast him from the mountain of God to the ground. The poem ends with the king as a warning to other rulers.

The lament mixes two pictures. One is a real king growing rich through trade. The other is a shining being in Eden who is thrown down. Readers have argued for centuries about how these two pictures fit together.

words.d: a sad poem or song, often mourning a death or a fall
a winged heavenly guardian in the Hebrew Bible, like those who guard Eden in Genesis 3:24

look.title: A King in Eden
look.text: Paraphrase of Ezekiel 28:13–17: You were in Eden, the garden of God, covered with precious stones. You were an anointed cherub on God's holy mountain. You were blameless until wrong was found in you. Your heart grew proud because of your beauty, so I threw you to the ground.
look.prompt: Which details fit a human king of a trading city? Which details sound like a being from God's heavenly court?

check.q: Who is Ezekiel's lament in chapter 28 about?
check.why: Ezekiel 28:12 directs the lament to the king of Tyre, a rich trading city on the coast.

check.q: In Ezekiel 28, why is the king thrown down?
choices: His heart grew proud because of his beauty
He refused to count his people
He wore dirty clothes before God
He built a tower in Babylon
check.why: Ezekiel 28:17 says the king's heart grew proud because of his beauty, so God cast him to the ground.

check.q: What is a cherub in the Hebrew Bible?
check.why: A cherub is a heavenly guardian. Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24.

lessons.title: Kings or a Fallen Spirit?
lessons.mainIdea: Readers see Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 as poems about human kings, about a fallen spirit, or, like Heiser, about kings pictured through the Eden rebel's story.
reading: Many Jewish readers and many modern scholars read both poems as being about human kings. Isaiah names Babylon; Ezekiel names Tyre. In their view, the heavenly language is poetry. It shows how high these kings raised themselves and how far they fell.

Many Christian readers, from early church writers such as Origen and Tertullian onward, also saw the fall of a spirit being in these poems. They read them as telling how Satan fell through pride. That is why the name Lucifer, from Isaiah 14, became a popular name for the devil.

Heiser took a middle path in The Unseen Realm (2015). He agreed that the poems are aimed at real human kings. But he argued they borrow the story of a divine rebel who was cast down. For Heiser, the pattern behind both poems was the rebel of *Eden*: a shining being who wanted to rise, and fell.
All three readings take the words seriously. They differ on how poetry works and on what the poets had in mind. A careful reader can explain each view and point to the verses each one leans on.

words.d: the garden of God in Genesis 2–3; Ezekiel 28:13 also names it
a reader's explanation of what a text means

look.title: Three Readings Side by Side
look.text: Reading A: The poems are about human kings; the heavenly words are poetic pictures. Reading B: The poems also describe Satan's fall through pride. Reading C (Heiser): The poems target human kings but use the older story of the Eden rebel as their pattern.
look.prompt: Pick one verse from Isaiah 14 or Ezekiel 28. Explain how each reading would handle it.

check.q: How do many Jewish readers and modern scholars read Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28?
choices: As laws for the Day of Atonement
As prayers of the high priest
check.why: Many read both as poems about real kings of Babylon and Tyre, with heavenly language used as poetry.

check.q: What pattern did Heiser see behind both poems?
choices: The story of the rebel in Eden
The story of the tower of Babel
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015) Heiser argued the poems target human kings but draw on the story of the Eden rebel who was cast down.

check.q: Why did Lucifer become a popular name for the devil?
choices: Christian readers linked Isaiah 14 to Satan's fall
The Hebrew Bible uses it as Satan's name in Job
Ezekiel calls the king of Tyre Lucifer
Jesus uses the name in the Gospels
check.why: Many Christian readers read Isaiah 14:12 as Satan's fall, so the KJV's word Lucifer became a name for the devil.

lessons.title: Belial and Mastema
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish writings from the Second Temple period gave the leader of evil spirits new names, such as Belial and Mastema.
reading: The *Second Temple period* runs from about 516 BCE, when the temple was rebuilt, to 70 CE, when the Romans destroyed it. In these centuries Jewish writers wrote many books outside the Hebrew Bible. Some of them gave names to a leader of evil powers.

One name is *Belial*. In the Hebrew Bible, beliyya'al is a word meaning worthlessness. The KJV prints phrases like "sons of Belial" for wicked men, as in 1 Samuel 2:12. In the Dead Sea Scrolls, Belial becomes a leader of evil. The War Scroll describes a coming battle of the sons of light against the sons of darkness, who belong to Belial.

Another name is *Mastema*, from a Hebrew word for hostility. The book of Jubilees, written around 160 BCE, calls him the chief of the spirits. In Jubilees 10, Noah prays against the evil spirits troubling his grandchildren. Mastema asks God to leave some spirits under his control. God allows a tenth to stay and binds the rest.

Paul uses the name Belial once. In 2 Corinthians 6:15 he asks what agreement Christ could have with Belial. Heiser argued that these writings show how Jewish thinking about a chief enemy grew between the two testaments.

words.d: the years from the rebuilding of the temple (about 516 BCE) to its destruction by Rome (70 CE)
from a Hebrew word for worthlessness; in the Dead Sea Scrolls, a name for the leader of evil
from a Hebrew word for hostility; in Jubilees, the chief of the evil spirits

look.title: How Long Ago? (Approximate)
look.cite: Common scholarly dates: Isaiah c. 700s BCE, Ezekiel c. 580s BCE, Zechariah c. 520 BCE, Jubilees c. 160 BCE, Revelation c. 95 CE
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Zechariah's visions and the writing of Jubilees? Why might ideas about the adversary change over that time?

check.q: Which book calls Mastema the chief of the spirits?
check.why: The book of Jubilees, written around 160 BCE, names Mastema as chief of the evil spirits.

check.q: In the Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll, who belongs to Belial?
choices: The sons of God in Job
check.why: The War Scroll describes the sons of light fighting the sons of darkness, who belong to Belial.

check.q: Where does Paul use the name Belial?
check.why: In 2 Corinthians 6:15 Paul asks what agreement Christ has with Belial.

lessons.title: Satan in the Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: In the Gospels, Satan and the devil are names for one enemy who tests Jesus and whose power Jesus says is ending.
reading: The Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell of Jesus being tested in the wilderness. In Matthew 4:1–11 the devil offers him bread, a leap from the temple and all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answers each time with words from Deuteronomy. The devil leaves.

Notice the offer of kingdoms. In Luke 4:6 the devil claims that authority over the kingdoms has been given to him. Heiser read this against Deuteronomy 32, where the nations were placed under other heavenly powers. Other readers see it as the devil's boast, not a true claim.

In Luke 10:18, when his followers return from their mission, Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. In John 12:31 he calls the devil the *ruler of this world* and says he will be cast out. The New Testament pictures Satan as a real enemy whose power is being broken.

Revelation 12 then shows a war in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is thrown down to the earth. Heiser argued that the New Testament gathers the threads of the Old: the serpent, the accuser, and the fallen king. It gives them one name.

words.d: Jesus's title for the devil in John 12:31, pointing to his claimed power over the world
a test that pulls someone toward doing wrong

look.title: Three Tellings of the Wilderness Test
look.cite: Verse counts from the standard chapter-and-verse divisions of the Gospels
look.prompt: Mark's telling is very short. What kinds of details might Matthew and Luke add in their longer tellings?

check.q: In Matthew 4, how does Jesus answer each of the devil's tests?
check.why: In Matthew 4:1–11 Jesus answers each test by quoting Deuteronomy, and the devil leaves.

check.q: What does Jesus say in Luke 10:18?
choices: He saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven
Satan is an officer of God's court
Belial rules the sons of darkness
The serpent was only an animal
check.why: In Luke 10:18 Jesus tells his returning followers he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

check.q: What does Jesus call the devil in John 12:31?
check.why: John 12:31 calls him the ruler of this world and says he will be cast out. Chief of the spirits is Jubilees' title for Mastema.

review.q: Which word best translates the Hebrew satan?
review.why: Satan means adversary or opponent. It can describe an angel, a king or a soldier.

review.q: In which two books does "the satan" act as an accuser in God's court?
review.why: Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 use ha-satan for an accuser who stands in God's heavenly court.

review.q: Which statement matches Heiser's view in Demons (2020)?
choices: The Old Testament uses satan as a role, not as a personal name
The satan in Job is the king of Tyre
Belial and Mastema appear in Genesis 3
The word devil comes from Hebrew
review.why: Heiser argued the Old Testament uses satan as a title or role. It becomes a personal name in the New Testament.

review.q: The KJV word Lucifer in Isaiah 14:12 comes from which language?
review.why: Lucifer is a Latin word for the morning star, meaning light-bringer. The Hebrew is helel ben shachar.

review.q: Which poem says the king was in Eden, the garden of God?
choices: Ezekiel 28, about the king of Tyre
Isaiah 14, about the king of Babylon
Job 1, about the court of God
review.why: Ezekiel 28:13 places the king of Tyre in Eden, the garden of God, and calls him a cherub.

review.q: Which name comes from the Greek word for slanderer?
review.why: Devil comes from diabolos, slanderer. Belial and Mastema are from Hebrew, and Lucifer is Latin.

review.q: How does Revelation 12:9 connect to Genesis 3?
choices: It names the king of Babylon
review.why: Revelation 12:9 calls the dragon that old serpent, the devil and Satan, linking him to the serpent of Eden.

review.q: What did Heiser see behind Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28?
choices: Human kings pictured through the Eden rebel's story
Only the story of Job's suffering
A list of Dead Sea Scroll names
Plain history with no poetry at all
review.why: Heiser read the poems as aimed at real kings but patterned on the older story of a divine rebel cast down from Eden.
